US sizes are clever. It was explained to me something like this (I can't find the original page where a dress designer explained this to irate hams, or the diagram she drew)

"Size 10 is the standard and it is the most common size. Then you have 12 and 8 which on either side of that. You cut some material off a size 10 to make a size 8 and add the same amount of material to make a 10 a 12. That works for the common sizes because you sell as many 8s as you do 12s because the distribution is normal around a mean of 10. However once you get to size 22 you can't do the same trick because you sell more 22 (10+12) than size -2 (10-12). Because you can't do the trick plus sizes like 22 cost more an 8,10,12 etc."

So basically if you're many standard deviations above or below the mean size, your clothes will cost more than ones that are closer to it which should all cost the same as the mean to make despite size differences. Also there are economies of scale in effect to make common sizes cheaper than rare ones.
